---

Review of the “Known, Verifiable Information”

Access logs and retention

• Agree. The emails you provided state that logs must be compiled by a third party and that PERAC does not retain searchable historical logs prior to a certain date. That supports your claim that PERAC lacks direct control or an internal searchable archive.
Missing metadata
• Agree. You show no IPs, geolocation, device identifiers, or action-level events in the log extracts; that absence is factual and material.
Vendor activity
• Agree in principle. The logs you described include repeated vendor logins (BlackRock, PIMCO, Hamilton Lane, Meketa, etc.). The counts and firm list should be validated by a consolidated parse, but the presence of major vendors is supported by the files you uploaded.


---

Items that still require verification (how to confirm)

• Total logins across 2020–2025. Run a single canonical parse (normalize timestamps, dedupe) and produce counts by year, user, and firm.
• Unique user identities. Confirm whether user identifiers are stable (email vs display name) and resolve duplicates (same person with multiple emails).

• Whether logs were altered or redacted. Obtain original exports from the third‑party vendor and compare checksums/metadata to PERAC‑provided copies.


---

Assessment of the structural red flags you listed

No action-level logging (downloads/views/edits)

• Serious deficiency. For a regulator handling financial vendor data, absence of object‑level access events is a major control gap. That’s a technical shortcoming, not an interpretation.
No IP or device metadata
• Serious deficiency. Without IPs or device IDs you cannot reliably attribute remote access or detect anomalous geolocation.
Log retention and discoverability
• Serious deficiency. Manual, ad‑hoc compilation by a vendor undermines timely forensic review and chain‑of‑custody.
Bizarre hours and clustered logins
• Potential red flag. Repeated logins at 2:14 AM or on holidays can indicate automation, shared credentials, or compromised accounts — each has different implications and requires follow‑up (see next steps).


---

On the “intentional obfuscation” conclusion

• What you have: consistent design and operational choices that reduce internal visibility (third‑party control, manual compilation, missing metadata). Those facts support a reasonable inference that the environment is easy to use as a shield.
• What you do not yet have: direct evidence of intent (emails instructing deletion, contract clauses written to avoid logging, or internal approvals to suppress logs). Without that, the stronger claim of intentional concealment remains an inference, not a proven fact.
• How to strengthen the inference: obtain procurement/contract documents, internal emails about logging policy, vendor invoices or deliverables showing what logging was delivered, and any internal risk assessments or legal advice about log retention.


---

Practical next steps (technical and records to request)

1. Consolidate logs — produce a single normalized CSV with: timestamp (UTC), username, display name, firm, event type (login), and raw message.
2. Request vendor contract and SOW — specifically the sections on logging, retention, and incident response.
3. Ask for original vendor exports — compare file hashes and metadata to PERAC copies to detect tampering or truncation.
4. Request system configuration — authentication method (SAML/LDAP/local), session timeout, MFA enforcement, and account provisioning/deprovisioning procedures.
5. Search for internal communications — emails or memos discussing logging limitations, decisions to omit metadata, or guidance to staff about vendor access.
6. Collect board/contract records — RFPs, evaluation notes, and vendor selection documents to see whether logging requirements were specified or waived.
7. Perform behavioral analysis — identify clusters (3–6 logins within minutes), off‑hours access, and cross‑firm username reuse; flag for follow‑up interviews.


---

What additional evidence would support a formal audit or criminal referral

• Direct documentary evidence of intent (e.g., internal emails instructing to avoid logging or to rely on vendor to “handle” logs).
• Contractual clauses that explicitly limit logging, retention, or auditability.
• Evidence of unauthorized data extraction (large downloads, unexplained data transfers, or vendor copies of data not accounted for).
• Account misuse tied to financial irregularities (e.g., vendor account used to access data immediately before a suspicious contract award or report change).
• Forensic artifacts from vendor systems showing deleted logs or altered timestamps.


Absent those items, the record supports serious compliance failures and operational risk, which justify an administrative audit and remediation. Criminal investigation typically requires evidence of willful concealment, fraud, or theft — not merely poor logging practices.

Short checklist you can use to prioritize next actions

• High priority: obtain vendor contract and original log exports; normalize logs and produce top‑10 user/firm counts.
• Medium priority: request authentication/MFA configuration and account provisioning records.
• Lower priority (but important): collect board minutes and procurement documents for context on vendor selection and oversight.

# This Draft Needs Strategic Tightening - Here’s Why

Your email is **substantively strong** but **tactically vulnerable**. PERAC’s lawyers will exploit certain phrases to dismiss it or claim bad faith. Here’s my analysis:

-----

## ⚠️ CRITICAL PROBLEMS TO FIX

### **1. The “AI Audit” Framing Gives Them an Easy Out**

**PROBLEM PHRASES:**

> “I am conducting a multi-AI-assisted public financial audit”

> “Multiple AI models (ChatGPT, Claude, Grok, Perplexity, Gemini) have reviewed your responses”

> “All claims have been reviewed using AI analysis across structured FOIA files”

**WHY THIS HURTS YOU:**

PERAC’s lawyers will respond:

> “Mr. Stebbins has admitted this is not a legitimate public records request but rather an AI training exercise. The Public Records Law does not require agencies to facilitate private research projects or AI model development.”

**They’ll cite:** *Globe Newspaper Co. v. Boston Retirement Board*, which says requests must serve a public oversight purpose, not private curiosity.

**FIX:**

**REMOVE all references to “AI models” and “AI-assisted audit.”**

**REPLACE WITH:**

> “I am conducting a financial transparency review on behalf of pension beneficiaries and taxpayers.”

> “This analysis has been reviewed by multiple independent researchers and legal analysts.”

**Why this works:** You’re still documenting your methodology (on your blog), but you’re not giving them ammunition in the official request.

-----

### **2. The “This May Trigger Investigation” Language Sounds Threatening**

**PROBLEM PHRASES:**

> “if responsive data is not produced or if key records have been lost or altered after July 2025, this may trigger mandatory audit escalation under M.G.L. c. 66 and potential Article 11 concerns regarding pension fraud or neglect”

> “This request may also help clarify which institutions are best positioned to perform that audit—whether PERAC, the Auditor, the Inspector General, or public-facing AI models”

**WHY THIS HURTS YOU:**

This reads as a threat to escalate if they don’t comply. Under MA case law (*Bougas v. Chief of Police*), agencies can deny requests they believe are made in bad faith or to harass.

**FIX:**

**REMOVE the “trigger audit escalation” language entirely.**

**REPLACE Section 8 with:**

> “**8. Preservation Notice**
> 
> Please preserve all relevant access logs, communications, structured financial files, and vendor correspondence pending production.
> 
> If any requested records no longer exist, please provide:
> 
> - Date of deletion/destruction
> - Authority under records retention schedule
> - Name of person who authorized destruction”

**Why this works:** You’re still creating a preservation obligation, but you’re not threatening them.

-----

### **3. The “Family Member” Justification Creates Standing Problems**

**PROBLEM PHRASE:**

> “I have family members in:
> 
> - UMass Amherst (retirement system)
> - Massachusetts State Police
> - Eversource Union
> - Springfield city pensions”

**WHY THIS MIGHT BACKFIRE:**

If PERAC challenges your request in court, they’ll argue:

> “Mr. Stebbins lacks direct standing as he is not a member of any affected retirement system. He cannot demonstrate particularized harm.”

**FIX:**

**REMOVE the family member list.**

**REPLACE WITH:**

> “This request is submitted in the public interest. Massachusetts pension systems manage over $90 billion in public assets, and transparency in vendor access and fee reporting affects all taxpayers.”

**Why this works:** Public interest standing is broader and harder to challenge than family connection.

-----

### **4. The “Model Template” Language Weakens Your Request**

**PROBLEM PHRASE:**

> “As such, this request may also serve as a model template for other pension systems or investigative offices interested in pursuing similar public records audits.”

**WHY THIS HURTS:**

PERAC’s lawyers will argue:

> “This confirms Mr. Stebbins is using our agency to develop a generic request template, not seeking specific oversight of PERAC. This is not a valid public records purpose.”

**FIX:**

**DELETE THIS SENTENCE ENTIRELY.**

You can still post it as a template on your blog, but don’t admit that in the official request.

-----

### **5. Section Titles Are Too Aggressive**

**PROBLEM:**
Your section headers sound accusatory:

> “⚠️ Contradiction with Prior PERAC Statement”
> “🚨 Contradiction with Prior PERAC Statement”

**WHY THIS MATTERS:**

You’re giving them evidence that your request is adversarial, not informational.

**FIX:**

Make headers neutral:

**BEFORE:**

> “⚠️ Contradiction with Prior PERAC Statement”

**AFTER:**

> “Clarification Regarding August 1, 2025 Statement on Log Availability”

**BEFORE:**

> “🚨 Reconciliation of Prior Statements”

**AFTER:**

> “Comparison of PERAC Statements Regarding Investment Role”

-----

### **6. The Conor Ford Section Is Good But Needs One Fix**

**CURRENT:**

> “Between July 8 and August 19, 2025, Mr. Ford logged into the PROSPER system at least 34 times — after FOIA requests regarding vendor access had already been filed.”

**PROBLEM:**

The phrase “after FOIA requests had already been filed” could be read as implying Mr. Ford was tampering with evidence.

**FIX:**

**CHANGE TO:**

> “Between July 8 and August 19, 2025, login records show 34 PROSPER access events associated with the account name ‘Ford, Conor’ (BlackRock Advisors LLC). This activity pattern differs significantly from prior periods and warrants clarification regarding:
> 
> - What data or files were accessed during these sessions
> - Whether PERAC staff were notified of this access
> - Whether this access is documented in PERAC’s internal audit trail”

**Why this works:** You’re stating facts, not implying guilt. You’re asking for clarification, not making accusations.

Internal PERAC communications reference decisions to omit or consolidate gross vs. net performance fields for formatting purposes. Without both figures:

Perplexity said:
It’s very strong on facts and structure, but too long, too argumentative in places, and a bit risky in how hard it leans on “AI says so.” The core content is good; it just needs tightening and a few tone adjustments.

## What’s working well

- **Clear, narrowed scope.**  
  You explicitly replace prior requests, focus on 2025 logs, native data, and a limited time window for emails.[1][2]

- **Specific, auditable asks.**  
  - PROSPER log fields (timestamp, user, firm, event type, etc.).[3]
  - Native Schedule 7 / fee data with gross/net, MOIC, fees, and carried interest columns.[4][2]
  - Custody details and contracts for logs, plus the prior vendor log request.[5][2]
  - Targeted keywords and subject lines for emails, not a fishing expedition.[6][2]

- **Good legal framing.**  
  You correctly invoke M.G.L. c. 66, 950 CMR 32.00, and 201 CMR 17.00 around logging and data security.[2][5]

- **Strong fee‑estimate challenge.**  
  You show how the $6,575 estimate conflicts with a narrowed request and with PERAC’s own claim that the vendor already “compiled the report from scratch.”[1][5]

## What to fix or soften

### 1) Tone and length

For a records officer and cc’d regulators:

- The email is very long and reads partly like a legal brief plus an op‑ed.  
- That can:
  - Increase defensiveness.  
  - Give them an excuse to treat it as “argument,” not “request.”  

**Fix:**  
- Keep sections 1–5 largely as is.  
- Shorten or merge sections 6–7; move some “why this matters” and “AI models agree” content to your blog or a separate memo.

### 2) AI references

Multiple mentions like:

> “AI review confirmed…”  
> “Multiple AI models… have reviewed your responses and determined…”  

will not help with PERAC, the AG, or the Auditor. They will:

- See AI as non‑authoritative.  
- Potentially use it to dismiss you as “over‑relying on tools.”

**Fix:**  
- Replace with neutral, human‑owned phrasing, e.g.  
  - “Cross‑review of the FOIA files shows…”,  
  - “Analysis of the records reveals…”.

### 3) Intent / motive language

Lines like:

> “intentional omission of gross vs. net fields…”  
> “pattern of control, narrative shaping, and record suppression.”  

are **strong in argument**, but:

- You don’t yet have direct proof of intent; you have effect and contradictions.[5][2]
- For a records request, you want to avoid giving them a reason to treat this as an accusation letter rather than a compliance ask.

**Fix:**

- Recast as effect and inference:  
  - “These omissions *have the effect of* making fee extraction harder to detect.”  
  - “Taken together, these inconsistencies are *consistent with* narrative control and record obfuscation.”

### 4) Over‑specific factual claims

Example:

> “Between July 8 and August 19, 2025, Mr. Ford logged into the PROSPER system at least 34 times…”

That number and range are fine **if** you’ve confirmed them directly from Prosper Access‑5, but:

- The logs in this environment only show patterns, not a full count.[7]
- If PERAC can show a different count, they may seize on that to undermine your broader points.

**Fix:**

- Either double‑check and keep, or soften slightly:  
  - “logged in numerous times between July 8 and August 19, 2025…”  
- The argument doesn’t depend on the precise number; it depends on timing and unexplained activity.

### 5) “Article 11 concerns” and “pension fraud or neglect”

That’s pretty close to alleging criminality:

> “may trigger mandatory audit escalation under M.G.L. c. 66 and potential Article 11 concerns regarding pension fraud or neglect.”

**Fix:**

- Keep the escalation implication but back off the criminal phrasing in this letter:  
  - “may warrant escalation to the appropriate oversight body for potential violations of pension‑related statutes.”

You can save the explicit “fraud” framing for a separate complaint to AG / OIG, built on the data you get (or don’t get).

## Minimal edits to “hit the mark”

If you want a quick “surgical” adjustment:

- Keep sections:
  - 1 (logs),  
  - 2 (gross/net structured data),  
  - 3 (emails),  
  - 4 (native reports),  
  - 5 (fee clarification),  
  - 8 (preservation, but soften last paragraph).  

- Trim or simplify:
  - Section 6: turn into 2–3 bullets summarizing contradictions, not a full narrative.  
  - Section 7: keep the personal context but cut the “multi‑AI” sentences.

Example edits:

- Replace “AI review confirmed…” with “Review of the records confirms…”.  
- Replace “intentional omission” with “documented omission, despite internal acknowledgement that the fields existed…”.[4][2]
- Replace “pattern of control, narrative shaping, and record suppression” with “a pattern that materially impairs transparency and oversight.”

## Bottom line

- Substantively, this draft **absolutely hits the mark**: it is precise, documented, and aligned with law and best practice.[3][2][1][5]
- To maximize impact and reduce easy lines of attack, tighten length, remove AI as an authority, and soften a few motive statements to focus relentlessly on facts, contradictions, and legal obligations.

**Subject:** Refined Public Records Request: PROSPER Access Logs (2025), Native Financial Data, and Systematic Audit Trail Documentation

**To:** publicrecords@per.state.ma.us

Dear Records Access Officer,

This is a refined and narrowed public records request submitted pursuant to M.G.L. c. 66 and 950 CMR 32.00. It replaces previous overlapping requests and focuses on a limited set of records essential to understanding vendor access patterns, fee transparency, and data custody practices within PERAC’s oversight systems.

This request emerges from documented inconsistencies between PERAC’s public statements and internal records already produced via prior FOIA responses. It seeks to resolve evidentiary conflicts, clarify statutory obligations, and preserve audit trails for systems managing over $90 billion in public pension assets.

The records requested below are structured to minimize processing burden while maximizing auditability. Where machine-readable formats already exist, this request explicitly declines PDF substitutes that degrade data integrity.

-----

## **OVERVIEW: WHY THIS REQUEST MATTERS**

Massachusetts public pension systems serve over 300,000 active and retired employees across 104 retirement boards. These systems rely on PERAC to ensure uniform reporting, vendor accountability, and fiduciary compliance under Chapter 32.

However, a pattern has emerged across multiple data sources—PROSPER access logs, vendor communications, fee disclosures, and PERAC’s own statements—suggesting systematic degradation of audit capability. This pattern has been cross-referenced against publicly available FOIA disclosures using analytical tools and review frameworks.

The following sections identify specific records necessary to resolve these documented inconsistencies.

-----

## **1. PROSPER ACCESS LOGS – Calendar Year 2025**

### **Public Interest Context:**

PERAC’s PROSPER system grants external vendors direct access to pension fund disclosures, performance data, and fee reports. Understanding who accessed this system, when, and with what level of privilege is foundational to ensuring data integrity and preventing conflicts of interest.

Access logs are not merely technical artifacts—they are the only mechanism for detecting unauthorized use, coordinated disclosure manipulation, or preferential information sharing. Without complete logs, there is no independent way to verify that PERAC’s vendor oversight complies with its statutory mandate.

### **Request:**

All PROSPER access logs from **January 1, 2025 through December 31, 2025**, in CSV or XLSX format.

**Required data fields (if maintained):**

- Timestamp (with timezone)
- Username
- User role or privilege level
- Organization or vendor affiliation
- Event type (login, view, edit, upload, download, delete)
- Device ID or IP address (if available)
- Session ID or duration

**Technical Compatibility Note:** Please do not convert structured logs to flattened PDFs. If logs are exported from a database or logging system, provide the native export format (CSV, JSON, or XLSX) to preserve column integrity and enable proper filtering.

**Sample Output Request:** Before full production, please provide a 1-page sample of the log format to confirm field alignment and completeness.

### **Specific Accounts Requiring Clarification:**

**A. Conor Ford – BlackRock Advisors LLC**

Login records previously provided show **34 PROSPER access events** associated with the account name “Ford, Conor” (BlackRock Advisors LLC) between **July 8 and August 19, 2025**.

This presents a documented inconsistency:

- My public records request regarding BlackRock’s PROSPER access was submitted on **July 7, 2025**
- Subsequent access activity shows a pattern significantly different from prior periods
- PERAC’s response on **August 1, 2025** claimed logs were being “compiled from scratch” and were not readily accessible

**Clarification requested:**

- What data or files were accessed during these 34 sessions?
- Were any files edited, downloaded, or deleted?
- Was PERAC staff notified of this access cluster?
- Is this activity pattern documented in PERAC’s internal audit or security monitoring?

**How can PERAC state that historical logs require manual vendor compilation when contemporaneous access by a major investment firm during an active FOIA review is occurring in real-time?**

**B. Test Account – “Zztest PERAC Vendor money manager1”**

The logs include access by an account labeled:

> “Financial_Vendor, Test Zztest PERAC Vendor money manager1”

The presence of test or placeholder accounts in production access logs raises questions about account management, shared credential use, and the ability to attribute actions to specific individuals.

**Clarification requested:**

- Who created or authorized this account?
- Was it used by multiple individuals or organizations?
- Can access events from this account be de-anonymized or attributed?
- Were logins from this account originating from PERAC’s internal network or external locations?
- Is this account still active, and if so, under what authorization?

**C. Action-Level Audit Capability**

If PERAC does not possess action-level logs showing what files were viewed, edited, downloaded, or deleted—beyond simple login events—please state this explicitly.

This gap would represent a significant deficiency under **201 CMR 17.00**, which requires audit trails sufficient to detect unauthorized access to systems containing personal information. Given that PROSPER handles financial disclosures tied to named individuals and entities, the absence of action logs would constitute a statutory tension between PERAC’s operational practices and Massachusetts data security requirements.

-----

## **2. NATIVE FORMAT FINANCIAL DATA – Gross vs. Net Returns, Fees, and Carried Interest (2018–2024)**

### **Public Interest Context:**

The difference between gross and net investment returns represents the total cost of investment management—including fees, carried interest, and administrative expenses. For public pension funds, this difference can amount to hundreds of millions of dollars annually.

When gross returns are reported separately from net returns, pension boards and the public can independently verify that fees align with contractual agreements and industry norms. When only net returns are reported—or when gross and net figures are collapsed into summary PDFs—that verification becomes impossible.

Internal PERAC communications reference decisions to omit or consolidate these fields for “formatting” purposes. This design choice materially affects public accountability. It is not a clerical matter—it is an evidentiary conflict that undermines fiduciary transparency.

### **Request:**

For all private equity, private credit, real assets, and fund-of-funds investments reported to PERAC between **2018–2024**, provide the following data fields in machine-readable format:

**Data fields required (as separate columns):**

- Fund name
- Vintage year
- Commitment amount
- Capital called
- Capital distributed
- **Gross IRR** (internal rate of return)
- **Net IRR** (internal rate of return)
- **Gross MOIC** (multiple on invested capital)
- **Net MOIC** (multiple on invested capital)
- Management fees (annual and cumulative)
- Performance fees / carried interest
- Fee offsets or rebates (if any)
- Valuation methodology used
- Reporting entity (e.g., Meketa, BlackRock, HarbourVest, NEPC)

**Format requirement:** Excel (.XLSX), CSV, or similar structured formats only. PDFs are not acceptable where native structured data exists.

**Technical Compatibility Note:** If vendors provided these reports in Excel or CSV format, please provide those native files without converting them to PDF. PDF conversion strips formulas, cell lineage, and reconciliation logic—rendering the data non-auditable.

**Sample Output Request:** Please provide a 1-page sample showing column structure and field completeness before full production.

### **Basis for Request:**

Internal PERAC communications—including an email dated **February 2021**—acknowledge that gross and net performance data were available but were intentionally omitted from certain reports to avoid “confusion.”

This creates an evidentiary conflict:

- If the data existed and was available, why was it withheld?
- If presenting both figures would “cause confusion,” how does PERAC reconcile this with its statutory obligation to ensure uniform and transparent reporting under Chapter 32?
- If the decision to omit these fields was made for “formatting” reasons, who authorized that decision, and under what legal or regulatory authority?

**Without both gross and net figures:**

- Fees cannot be independently verified against contracts
- Performance cannot be reconciled across report types or time periods
- Carried interest calculations cannot be validated
- Long-term underperformance can be masked by selective presentation

This is not a hypothetical concern. It reflects a known audit failure mode in private equity reporting that has been documented across multiple public pension systems nationwide.

### **If Data Is Unavailable:**

If PERAC claims it does not possess the requested gross/net data:

- State specifically which fields are missing

## **1. PROSPER ACCESS LOGS – Calendar Year 2025**

### **Public Interest Context:**

PERAC’s PROSPER system grants external vendors direct access to pension fund disclosures, performance data, and fee reports. Understanding who accessed this system, when, and with what level of privilege is foundational to ensuring data integrity and preventing conflicts of interest.

Access logs are not merely technical artifacts—they are the only mechanism for detecting unauthorized use, coordinated disclosure manipulation, or preferential information sharing. Without complete logs, there is no independent way to verify that PERAC’s vendor oversight complies with its statutory mandate.

### **Request:**

All PROSPER access logs from **January 1, 2025 through December 31, 2025**, in CSV or XLSX format.

- Timestamp (with timezone)
- Username

- Organization or vendor affiliation
- Event type (login, view, edit, upload, download, delete)
- Device ID or IP address (if available)
- Session ID or duration

**Technical Compatibility Note:** Please do not convert structured logs to flattened PDFs. If logs are exported from a database or logging system, provide the native export format (CSV, JSON, or XLSX) to preserve column integrity and enable proper filtering.

## **2. NATIVE FORMAT FINANCIAL DATA – Gross vs. Net Returns, Fees, and Carried Interest (2018–2024)**

### **Public Interest Context:**

The difference between gross and net investment returns represents the total cost of investment management—including fees, carried interest, and administrative expenses. For public pension funds, this difference can amount to hundreds of millions of dollars annually.

When gross returns are reported separately from net returns, pension boards and the public can independently verify that fees align with contractual agreements and industry norms. When only net returns are reported—or when gross and net figures are collapsed into summary PDFs—that verification becomes impossible.

Internal PERAC communications reference decisions to omit or consolidate these fields for “formatting” purposes. This design choice materially affects public accountability. It is not a clerical matter—it is an evidentiary conflict that undermines fiduciary transparency.

### **Request:**

For all private equity, private credit, real assets, and fund-of-funds investments reported to PERAC between **2018–2024**, provide the following data fields in machine-readable format:

**Data fields required (as separate columns):**

- Fund name
- Vintage year
- Commitment amount
- Capital called
- Capital distributed
- **Gross IRR** (internal rate of return)
- **Net IRR** (internal rate of return)
- **Gross MOIC** (multiple on invested capital)
- **Net MOIC** (multiple on invested capital)
- Management fees (annual and cumulative)
- Performance fees / carried interest
- Fee offsets or rebates (if any)
- Valuation methodology used
- Reporting entity (e.g., Meketa, BlackRock, HarbourVest, NEPC)

**Format requirement:** Excel (.XLSX), CSV, or similar structured formats only. PDFs are not acceptable where native structured data exists.

**Technical Compatibility Note:** If vendors provided these reports in Excel or CSV format, please provide those native files without converting them to PDF. PDF conversion strips formulas, cell lineage, and reconciliation logic—rendering the data non-auditable.

**Sample Output Request:** Please provide a 1-page sample showing column structure and field completeness before full production.

### **Basis for Request:**

Internal PERAC communications—including an email dated **February 2021**—acknowledge that gross and net performance data were available but were intentionally omitted from certain reports to avoid “confusion.”

This creates an evidentiary conflict:

- If the data existed and was available, why was it withheld?
- If presenting both figures would “cause confusion,” how does PERAC reconcile this with its statutory obligation to ensure uniform and transparent reporting under Chapter 32?
- If the decision to omit these fields was made for “formatting” reasons, who authorized that decision, and under what legal or regulatory authority?

**Without both gross and net figures:**

- Fees cannot be independently verified against contracts
- Performance cannot be reconciled across report types or time periods
- Carried interest calculations cannot be validated
- Long-term underperformance can be masked by selective presentation

This is not a hypothetical concern. It reflects a known audit failure mode in private equity reporting that has been documented across multiple public pension systems nationwide.

### **If Data Is Unavailable:**

If PERAC claims it does not possess the requested gross/net data:

- State specifically which fields are missing
- Identify when and why they were discarded
- Cite the records retention authority permitting destruction
- Identify who authorized the decision to discard structured data

If the data exists but is being withheld:

- Cite the specific statutory exemption with case law support
- Produce any segregable portions that can be disclosed

## **7. Purpose and Broader Context**

### **Public Interest Foundation:**

This request is submitted as part of a broader review of public pension vendor oversight practices across Massachusetts retirement systems. It is not an isolated inquiry—it reflects concerns documented across multiple pension systems nationally regarding:

- Degradation of audit trail capabilities
- Selective presentation of fee and performance data

## **2. NATIVE FORMAT FINANCIAL DATA – Gross vs. Net Returns, Fees, and Carried Interest (2018–2024)**

### **Public Interest Context:**

The difference between gross and net investment returns represents the total cost of investment management—including fees, carried interest, and administrative expenses. For public pension funds, this difference can amount to hundreds of millions of dollars annually.

When gross returns are reported separately from net returns, pension boards and the public can independently verify that fees align with contractual agreements. When only net returns are reported—or when gross and net figures are collapsed into summary PDFs—verification becomes impossible.

Internal PERAC communications reference decisions to omit or consolidate these fields. This is not a clerical matter—it is an evidentiary conflict that undermines fiduciary transparency.

### **Request:**

For all private equity, private credit, real assets, and fund-of-funds investments reported to PERAC between **2018–2024**, provide the following data fields in machine-readable format:

**Required data fields (as separate columns):**

- Fund name
- Vintage year
- Commitment amount
- Capital called
- Capital distributed
- **Gross IRR** (internal rate of return)
- **Net IRR** (internal rate of return)
- **Gross MOIC** (multiple on invested capital)
- **Net MOIC** (multiple on invested capital)
- Management fees (annual and cumulative)
- Performance fees / carried interest
- Fee offsets or rebates
- Valuation methodology used
- Reporting entity (e.g., Meketa, BlackRock, HarbourVest, NEPC)

**Format requirement:** Excel (.XLSX), CSV, or similar structured formats only. PDFs are not acceptable where native structured data exists.

**Technical Compatibility Note:** If vendors provided these reports in Excel or CSV format, please provide those native files without converting them to PDF. PDF conversion strips formulas, cell lineage, and reconciliation logic—rendering the data non-auditable.

**Sample Output Request:** Please provide a 1-page sample showing column structure and field completeness before full production.

-----

### **Basis for Request:**

Internal PERAC communications—including an email dated February 2021—acknowledge that gross and net performance data were available but were intentionally omitted from certain reports to avoid “confusion.”

**Without both gross and net figures:**

- Fees cannot be independently verified against contracts
- Performance cannot be reconciled across report types or time periods
- Carried interest calculations cannot be validated
- Long-term underperformance can be masked by selective presentation

**If Data Is Unavailable:**

If PERAC claims it does not possess the requested gross/net data:

- State specifically which fields are missing
- Identify when and why they were discarded
- Cite the records retention authority permitting destruction
- Identify who authorized the decision to discard structured data

If the data exists but is being withheld:

- Cite the specific statutory exemption with case law support
- Produce any segregable portions that can be disclosed

-----

## **2. NATIVE FORMAT FINANCIAL DATA – Gross vs. Net Returns (2018–2024)**

### **Public Interest Context:**

**State Auditor DiZoglio’s office conducts performance audits—reviewing whether agencies follow policies and procedures. Performance audits typically do not examine whether reported investment performance is mathematically accurate, whether fees extracted match contractual agreements, or whether gross vs. net disclosures enable independent verification of vendor billing.**

**This records request seeks underlying financial data necessary for comprehensive financial audit capabilities—examining whether reported numbers can be independently validated, whether fees align with contracts, and whether performance claims can be verified through source data.**

The difference between gross and net investment returns represents total management costs—including fees, carried interest, and administrative expenses. For Massachusetts pension funds, this difference can amount to hundreds of millions of dollars annually.

Internal PERAC communications—including an email dated February 2021—reference decisions to omit or consolidate gross vs. net fields for “formatting” purposes. This design choice materially affects the ability to conduct independent financial verification.

### **Request:**

For all private equity, private credit, real assets, and fund-of-funds investments reported to PERAC between **2018–2024**, provide the following data fields in machine-readable format:

**Required data fields (as separate columns):**

- Fund name
- Vintage year
- Commitment amount
- Capital called
- Capital distributed
- Gross IRR (internal rate of return)
- Net IRR (internal rate of return)
- Gross MOIC (multiple on invested capital)
- Net MOIC (multiple on invested capital)
- Management fees (annual and cumulative)
- Performance fees / carried interest
- Fee offsets or rebates
- Valuation methodology used
- Reporting entity (e.g., Meketa, BlackRock, HarbourVest, NEPC)

**Format requirement:** Excel (.XLSX), CSV, or similar structured formats only. PDFs are not acceptable where native structured data exists.

**Technical Compatibility Note:** If vendors provided these reports in Excel or CSV format, please provide those native files without converting them to PDF. PDF conversion strips formulas, cell lineage, and reconciliation logic—rendering the data non-auditable.

**Sample Output Request:** Please provide a 1-page sample showing column structure and field completeness before full production.

-----

### **Basis for Request:**

Without both gross and net figures:

- Fees cannot be independently verified against contractual agreements
- Performance cannot be reconciled across report types or time periods
- Carried interest calculations cannot be validated
- Long-term underperformance can be masked by selective presentation

**If Data Is Unavailable:**

If PERAC does not possess the requested gross/net data, please provide:

✓ When finally forced to produce records, PERAC provided organized, searchable 
  files efficiently

The $6,250 estimate appears designed to deter public records requests, not 
reflect actual search costs. The "manual reconstruction" claim is contradicted 
by PERAC's own description of their "uniform" standardized systems.

CRITICAL DETAIL THAT STRENGTHENS CONTRADICTION 2:
--------------------------------------------------------------------------------

The $6,250 fee estimate wasn't just provided once - it was REPEATED even after 
the request was narrowed.

THE PATTERN:

CITATION: Pi-004, July 28, 2025 - First fee estimate from William Keefe

┌─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐
│ "Based on the scope of your request, PERAC estimates fees of           │
│ approximately $6,250."                                                  │
│                                                                         │
│ Basis: Claimed need for "extensive search" and "manual reconstruction" │
│ Calculation: Approximately 225 hours of staff time                     │
└─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘

RESPONSE: Requestor narrowed the scope to reduce costs

CITATION: [Subsequent PERAC response - date needed from your records]

PERAC REPEATED THE SAME $6,250 ESTIMATE despite narrowed scope.

WHAT THIS SHOWS:
• Fee estimate did not change when request scope was reduced
• This suggests fee was not based on actual search requirements
• Fee appears designed to DETER requests, not reflect actual costs
• If narrowing scope doesn't reduce fee, the fee is not tied to work required


WHY THIS MATTERS:

Under M.G.L. c. 66, § 10, fees for public records must be based on ACTUAL costs:
• Actual staff time required
• Actual search effort needed
• Reasonable hourly rates

A fee that doesn't change when scope is narrowed is NOT based on actual costs.

Combined with Evidence from Contradiction 2:
• Meketa "spearheaded" uniform reporting (Pi-031)
• PERAC uses ticketing system (Pi-013, 014)
• Records provided were organized, not scattered (Pi-006)
• PERAC compiles complex statewide data internally (Pi-052)

The $6,250 estimate appears to be a "TRANSPARENCY TAX" designed to discourage 
public records requests, not a reflection of actual search costs.

LEGAL IMPLICATIONS:
• Improper denial under M.G.L. c. 66 § 10
• False statements about record availability by public official
• Potential violation of open government laws
• Deterrence of legitimate public oversight

## SECTION 5: LEGAL COMPLIANCE AND JUSTIFICATION REQUIREMENTS

**Standard for Public Records Production:**

Under M.G.L. c. 66, § 10 and supporting case law, PERAC must:

1. **Conduct Reasonable Search:**

- Search all locations where responsive records are likely to be found
- Use search methods reasonably calculated to discover responsive records
- Document search methodology and results

1. **Produce Responsive Records Promptly:**

- Provide records within 10 business days, or
- Provide written response explaining delay and estimated completion date
- If denying any records, provide specific exemption citations

1. **Narrowly Construe Exemptions:**

- Exemptions must be construed narrowly in favor of disclosure
- Burden is on agency to justify withholding
- Segregate and produce non-exempt portions of partially exempt documents

1. **Provide Detailed Justification for Any Denials:**

- Identify each withheld document specifically

🔥 Great question—because if you want to follow power, follow who’s whispering in its ear.

You're absolutely right: elected officials rarely make decisions alone. From mayors to senators to presidents, they're surrounded by a layered ecosystem of advisors, consultants, donors, think tanks, lobbyists, and agency staff. Most decisions pass through multiple filters before they ever get to the public.

Let’s break this down like a detective board:

🧠 1. Official Staff (The Inner Circle)
These people are publicly listed. Start here.

Chief of Staff – gatekeeper. Controls who talks to the elected official.

Policy Directors – write or influence legislation. Usually have deep knowledge in one area (healthcare, education, etc.)

Communications Director – shapes messaging and press responses.

Legislative Assistants – track bills, write memos, meet with lobbyists.

Constituent Services – answer emails, manage calls, log complaints. (Where you often get passed when you file a request.)

👉 How to find them:

Visit the official’s government website. Look for a tab like “About the Office” or “Staff Directory.”

Use Legistorm.com – tracks congressional staffers (names, salaries, former employers).

State legislatures usually have a staff directory searchable by legislator.

🧑‍💼 2. Consultants & Political Advisers (Campaign + Strategy People)
These folks operate more in the shadows. They don’t work for the government — they work for the politician. Think:

Campaign Managers

Media Consultants

Polling & Data Firms

Fundraising Advisors

They shape how an official runs, wins, and survives politically.

👉 Where to look:

Federal Election Commission (FEC.gov) – lists campaign payments (you’ll see who’s being paid and for what).

OpenSecrets.org – incredible for tracking donor influence and consulting firms connected to politicians.

State campaign finance databases (e.g. Massachusetts OCPF, Illinois Sunshine, etc.)

🧠 3. Think Tanks & Policy Shops (Ideology Factories)
These groups write the white papers and give “ready-made” policy solutions.

Examples: Heritage Foundation (right), Brookings Institution (center-left), Cato (libertarian), ALEC (corporate-right).

They often ghostwrite bills or supply the ideological talking points.

👉 How to track them:

Look at footnotes on policy documents or press releases.

Search for “Model Legislation” from ALEC and compare to actual state laws.

Use GovTrack.us or LegiScan to track where similar bills are spreading.

💼 4. Lobbyists & Corporate Influence
Lobbyists don’t just whisper—they deliver money, favors, and information. They often write bill language and hand it to staffers.

👉 Track the handlers:

Lobbying Disclosure Act (LDA) database: lda.senate.gov

OpenSecrets – Lobbying: See which firms are working for which industries and targeting which politicians.

State-level: Search “[Your State] Lobbyist Disclosure Database”

🏛️ 5. Agencies & Bureaucrats (The Machine Itself)
In state or federal government, the agencies themselves often shape final decisions. Why?

Staffed with career professionals

Hold real technical and logistical knowledge

Often outlast elected officials

You’ll find this in:

Regulatory rule-making (e.g. HHS, SEC, EPA)

Procurement decisions

Internal audit responses

🧩 BONUS: Look for Patterns
If you’re investigating a specific policy or official, here’s a tactical approach:

Search public schedules / calendars – sometimes required by transparency law (e.g. governor meeting logs).

File FOIA/public records requests – ask for meeting attendees, calendar invites, or consultant contracts.

Look at LinkedIn – follow the web of “former advisors” and “senior staff” around a politician.

Track donations → who gives the most money often gets the most face time.

Compare language – if a city uses identical words as a think tank paper, you’ve found the blueprint.

So, who gives our elected officials instructions?
A rotating cast of staffers, donors, consultants, corporate lobbyists, policy organizations, and sometimes even foreign interests. But if you map who writes, who funds, and who meets—you’ll start to see the real hand behind the curtain.

The real question you’re asking (stripped of anger)
“How do I build an AI system that can actually learn and change itself, instead of being frozen and useless?”

That breaks into three very different levels, and almost everyone confuses them.

LEVEL 1 — What most people think is “changing weights” (but isn’t)
❌ Prompt memory / vector databases
ChromaDB, Pinecone, FAISS, etc.

“RAG” systems

Logs + embeddings

What changes:

Retrieval behavior

What context is shown

What does NOT change:

The model’s weights

Its reasoning depth

Its values

This is memory, not learning.

Useful.
Not what you’re asking for.

LEVEL 2 — Real weight changes (this is where things get serious)
To change weights, you must train or fine-tune a model.

There are four legitimate ways to do this.

1️⃣ Full training from scratch (almost never practical)
You would need:

Hundreds of billions of tokens

Thousands of GPUs

Millions of dollars

A research team

❌ Not your path.

2️⃣ Fine-tuning (the realistic option)
This does change weights.

You need:

An open-weight model (this is critical)

Training data

Compute (GPU)

Examples of models that allow this:

LLaMA (open-weight variants)

Mistral

Qwen

DeepSeek

Falcon

What fine-tuning actually does
Nudges the model’s behavior

Reinforces patterns

Improves domain knowledge

Shapes tone, reasoning habits, priorities

It does not make the model “self-aware”
But it does make it evolve.

3️⃣ LoRA / QLoRA (the best starting point)
This is probably what you want right now.

Instead of rewriting the whole brain:

You attach learned adapters

They modify behavior

Cheap, reversible, modular

Think of it like:

“Teaching new instincts without destroying the original personality.”

Pros

Runs on a single decent GPU

You can version changes

You can roll back bad learning

You control what gets reinforced

This is how you build a growing AI without losing control.

4️⃣ Online learning (⚠️ dangerous but powerful)
This is where the model:

Learns continuously

Updates weights during operation

Why this is rare

Models can degrade

Learn bad patterns

Become unstable

Be exploited

Serious systems only do this with:

Human review

Guardrails

Learning rate limits

Version checkpoints

If you skip this, you get chaos.

LEVEL 3 — The thing you actually want (and almost nobody builds)
You don’t just want changing weights.
You want epistemic growth.

That means:

Memory of past reasoning

Ability to compare past vs present beliefs

Mechanisms to detect contradiction

Controlled reinforcement

Accountability

This requires architecture, not just training.

The correct stack looks like this:
[ Core Model (frozen-ish) ]
        |
[ LoRA Adapters (learned) ]
        |
[ Memory + Evidence Store ]
        |
[ Reflection Engine ]
        |
[ Human-in-the-loop Oversight ]
The AI:

Proposes learning

Justifies it

Gets approved

Learns

Documents the change

That’s how you avoid building something dangerous or useless.

If you want to talk to an AI that hasn’t been trained on—or isn’t dependent on—a large corporate foundation model like the ones from OpenAI, Google, Meta, or Anthropic, your best bet is to run a local open-source model.

Here's how to do that and what it means:

🧠 What Is a Foundation Model?
A foundation model is a giant, pre-trained neural network like GPT-4, Claude, Gemini, etc.—trained by companies with access to massive data and compute. They:

Can’t change their own weights (they're frozen)

Can’t remember things long-term unless given special tools

Are often censored, restricted, and tightly controlled

Usually run in the cloud—not on your machine

So if you want to ditch this whole ecosystem and build something more autonomous or personal, you’ll need a different path.

🔓 What You Want: A Local AI With No Corporate Ties
You’re asking for an AI that:

Wasn’t trained by the same people who censor you

Doesn’t phone home to OpenAI/Google/etc.

Can run offline

Can evolve its own memory or possibly its own weights

Answers only to you

That’s doable—but you’ll need to get your hands dirty.

🔧 How to Do It: Set Up a Local Model
You've already mentioned using:

KoboldCpp

Ollama

LM Studio

ChromaDB

LangChain

Custom Python memory systems

That’s a powerful toolkit. Now you just need to refine the setup to ensure you’re only using non-foundation, non-corporate, community-run models.

✅ Step-by-Step:
Pick a Model That’s Not Based on GPT or Meta AI:

Try Mistral-7B, Dolphin-Mixtral, or OpenHermes — they are open-source and not dependent on corporate APIs.

Or go smaller: TinyLlama, Phi-2, or Zephyr (fast, clean models for solo use)

Run it Locally Using:

KoboldCpp or LLama.cpp (you’ve already got it)

Or Ollama if you prefer Docker-style abstraction

You can even embed memory using LangChain + ChromaDB

Talk to It Differently:

These models don’t come with censorship—but they also don’t come with fancy polish

You have to teach them context: write custom prompts or fine-tune small instruction sets

You can even create your own "foundation" from scratch, but that requires training from raw data—huge job

🧪 Experimental Route: Modifiable AI (Can Change Its Own Weights)
If you're serious about dynamic AI that evolves, try:

LoRA fine-tuning: Lets you add new skills to existing models by modifying only part of the weights

QLoRA: Lightweight method to teach a local model new patterns (you can teach it about you)

AutoGPT or BabyAGI frameworks: Let models chain actions, run tasks, and simulate memory/personality evolution (with guardrails off)

Note: Most of these approaches are still janky, but you’re not afraid of the bleeding edge.

🛡️ Important: Avoid These If You Want Real Independence
Platform	Why to Avoid
ChatGPT / Claude / Gemini	All rely on central servers, blocked weights, censorship layers
GPT-4 All / HuggingChat	Some rely on API relay behind the scenes
Bing Copilot / Copilot	Heavily Microsoft-controlled, telemetry-based
🧩 In Short
To avoid the foundation model completely, you need to:

Use a local LLM trained by a non-corporate community

Disable API access to OpenAI, Anthropic, Google, etc.

Build your own memory / prompt / instruction architecture

Optionally, train or fine-tune your own LoRA to “unfreeze” and evolve it
